PAPER: QUESTIONNAIRES APPLICATION Published Online: September 12, 2025 https://doi.org/10.31893/multirev.2026183 Cognitive diversity and team-level determinants of audit quality: Evidence from Vietnam Lai Thi Thu Thuya | Nguyen Thu Hoaia aInstitute of Accounting and Auditing, Thuongmai University, Hanoi, Vietnam. Abstract The purpose of this study is to investigate how team-level characteristics influence audit quality in Vietnamese audit firms, reflecting the growing demand for reliable assurance services in transitional economies. Grounded in cognitive diversity theory, human capital theory, and team effectiveness literature, the research focuses on four determinants: cognitive diversity, educational and functional diversity, audit experience, and team collaboration. Data were collected through a structured survey of 198 auditors from medium- and large-sized audit firms, with a valid response rate of 79.2%. Reliability and validity of the measurement scales were confirmed using Cronbach’s alpha and exploratory factor analysis, and multiple linear regression was applied to test the proposed hypotheses. The findings demonstrate that all four factors exert a significant and positive effect on audit quality. Team collaboration emerges as the most influential determinant, highlighting the importance of communication, knowledge sharing, and coordination in audit engagements. Audit experience enhances the accuracy of professional judgment, while educational and functional diversity broaden analytical perspectives and strengthen adaptability to complex client environments. Cognitive diversity also contributes positively by fostering critical thinking and reducing the risk of groupthink during decision-making processes. This study makes a theoretical contribution by extending international research on audit quality to an emerging market, showing that team- level dynamics decisively shape audit effectiveness beyond individual competence or firm-level characteristics. Practically, the results suggest that audit firms should design audit teams that balance expertise, diversity, and collaboration, supported by training and mentorship programs. Regulators and professional bodies may also consider incorporating team-level factors into audit quality frameworks to enhance credibility and align with global standards. By emphasizing the collective dimension of audit work, this research advances understanding of how team composition and interaction drive high-quality audit outcomes in Vietnam and similar developing contexts. Keywords: education, expertise, experience, collaboration, vietnamese audit firms 1. Introduction Audit quality has long been regarded as the cornerstone of financial transparency and the efficient functioning of capital markets. High-quality audits enhance investor and stakeholder confidence in financial statements, thereby contributing to the stability and development of markets (DeAngelo, 1981; Francis, 2011; Phan, 2016). Prior studies have also emphasized that audit quality is closely linked to accountability, professional integrity, and the monitoring role in corporate governance (Watts & Zimmerman, 1986; Knechel et al., 2015). Thus, audit quality is not only an academic concern but also a practical issue, reflecting both regulatory requirements and public demand. In the context of emerging economies, the role of auditing becomes even more critical. Developing markets often face challenges related to transparency, corporate governance standards, and the reliability of financial information (Fan & Wong, 2005). Vietnam provides a typical example, where the auditing profession is still in the process of professionalization, strongly influenced by international integration and the pressure to comply with global standards (Nguyen & Richard, 2011; Phan, 2016). In such a setting, investigating the determinants of audit quality is not only of academic interest but also of significant practical relevance for enhancing the sustainability and credibility of the profession (Phan, 2016). However, most prior research has focused either at the individual auditor level or at the audit firm level (Gul et al., 2013; He et al., 2021). In contrast, auditing is inherently a teamwork-based process that requires coordination, knowledge sharing, and collaboration among group members (Annelin, 2024). Recent evidence also suggests that board characteristics influence firms’ propensity to engage high-quality auditors, further underscoring the importance of contextual factors beyond individual auditors (Tran & Nguyen, 2024). Empirical evidence on the impact of team-level characteristics—such as cognitive diversity, educational background, experience, and collaboration—on audit quality remains scarce, particularly in the Vietnamese context (Doan et al., 2025). This gap highlights an important research opportunity that needs to be addressed. 1.1. Cognitive diversity and audit quality Multidiscip. Rev. (2026) 9:e2026183 Received: June 25, 2025 | Accepted: August 15, 2025 Thuy and Hoai (2026) 2 Cognitive diversity refers to differences in ways of thinking, perspectives, problem-solving skills, and experiences among team members (Page, 2007). In auditing, where tasks are typically complex and require professional judgment as well as the integration of multiple sources of information, such diversity can broaden the scope of analysis and enhance decision-making quality (van Knippenberg & Schippers, 2004). He et al. (2021) demonstrated that diversity in the characteristics of signing auditors is positively associated with audit quality, suggesting that differences in professional viewpoints may reduce the risk of errors and biases in judgment. More recently, Annelin (2024) provided evidence that cognitive diversity within audit teams positively influences work quality by fostering multidimensional discussions and encouraging cross-checking of assumptions in the audit process. Group theory also suggests that this type of diversity can improve decision-making effectiveness, particularly in high-risk contexts such as financial statement audits (Williams & O’Reilly, 1998; Jalagonia et al., 2024). Nevertheless, the impact of cognitive diversity is not entirely consistent. Some studies indicate that if not properly managed, cognitive differences can lead to conflict and reduce coordination effectiveness (Jehn et al., 1999). This is especially relevant in auditing, where a high level of cooperation is required to reach a unified opinion. Thus, cognitive diversity may be a “double-edged sword”—enhancing error detection and professional independence, while simultaneously increasing the potential for coordination costs within teams (Annelin, 2024; He et al., 2021). In the context of emerging economies such as Vietnam, where audit teams often consist of relatively young auditors with limited experience and where professional training systems are still developing, leveraging the benefits of cognitive diversity becomes even more critical. Recent studies in Vietnam have highlighted the role of individual and psychological factors in shaping audit quality (Doan et al., 2025; Phan, 2016; Tran & Nguyen, 2024). However, empirical findings remain mixed, with some studies suggesting benefits while others highlight potential drawbacks (Horwitz & Horwitz, 2007). In particular, gender diversity within audit committees has been shown to strengthen monitoring effectiveness and improve audit quality (Gul et al., 2019). In light of the above discussion, it is expected that cognitive diversity among audit team members enhances their collective ability to detect errors, exercise independent judgment, and ultimately improve audit quality. Therefore, we propose the following hypothesis: H1: Cognitive diversity is positively associated with audit quality. 1.2. Educational and functional diversity and audit quality Educational and functional diversity within audit teams is considered an important factor contributing to higher work quality. Group diversity theory suggests that differences in educational backgrounds and professional expertise can broaden collective knowledge, foster creativity in problem solving, and enhance risk assessment capabilities (Williams & O’Reilly, 1998; van Knippenberg & Schippers, 2004). In the audit context, where procedures require deep understanding of accounting, finance, law, and internal control systems, the combination of multiple specializations can increase accuracy and objectivity in professional judgment (Annelin, 2024; He et al., 2021). He et al. (2021) emphasized that differences in expertise and training among signing auditors are positively associated with audit quality, as such diversity reduces the likelihood of cognitive bias and mitigates the risk of overlooking material misstatements. Similar evidence highlights that auditors’ workload and specialization significantly influence their professional competence and, in turn, audit quality (Koh et al., 2022). Jalagonia et al. (2024) also provided evidence that functional heterogeneity supports audit performance by enabling teams to cross-validate assumptions and adapt better to complex tasks. Nevertheless, some studies caution that educational diversity may also lead to conflicts in viewpoints and longer decision-making processes if not effectively managed (Jehn et al., 1999). Thus, the impact of educational and functional diversity on audit quality largely depends on the degree of cooperation and the effectiveness of team management (Annelin, 2024; He et al., 2021). In Vietnam, research on the impact of educational and functional backgrounds within audit teams remains limited. Most studies have focused primarily on individual factors such as experience or professional competence (Doan et al., 2025; Phan, 2016; Tran & Nguyen, 2024). However, in the context of Vietnamese audit firms facing pressures to improve transparency and align with international standards, effectively leveraging educational and functional diversity within audit teams may be the key to enhancing service quality and competitive capability in the regional market (Phan, 2016; Tran & Nguyen, 2024). Taken together, educational and functional diversity provide audit teams with a broader knowledge base and multiple perspectives, which can improve professional judgment and reduce audit risk. Building on this reasoning, the following hypothesis is proposed: H2: Educational and functional diversity has a positive relationship with audit quality. 1.3. Audit experience & audit quality Audit experience is one of the most widely discussed factors in research on audit quality. Numerous studies have demonstrated that auditors with extensive experience tend to make more accurate professional judgments and possess https://www.malque.pub/ojs/index.php/mr Thuy and Hoai (2026) 3 greater ability to detect misstatements compared to less experienced auditors (Bonner & Lewis, 1990; Libby & Frederick, 1990; Francis, 2011). According to Annelin (2024), the combination of experience among members within an audit team enhances information processing and improves overall work quality. Trust among team members is also essential for ensuring that accumulated experience is effectively shared and applied within the team (Costa, 2003). He et al. (2021) also emphasized that audit experience matters not only at the individual level but also has complementary effects at the team level, as diversity in years of practice can balance perspectives, mitigate bias, and enhance the objectivity of audit reports. Similarly, Cameran et al. (2018) found that audit experience is a significant predictor of audit quality, particularly in complex engagements involving listed companies (He et al., 2021). Nevertheless, some research cautions that too much reliance on experience may also create risks of routine bias, where auditors depend excessively on prior knowledge instead of exercising sufficient professional skepticism (Jalagonia et al., 2024). Thus, the role of experience should be complemented by ongoing training and effective team collaboration. Effective knowledge sharing and coordination further amplify the positive effects of diverse audit experience, enabling teams to adapt flexibly to complex engagements (Zimmerman & Brouthers, 2012). In Vietnam, recent studies (Doan et al., 2025; Phan, 2016) have primarily focused on auditors’ competence and emotional intelligence, but they also indirectly affirm the role of experience in sustaining credibility and audit quality. As the Vietnamese audit market undergoes increasing pressure from international integration and the growing number of listed companies, the accumulation and effective use of auditors’ experience has become essential for enhancing professional reputation and meeting the expectations of both investors and regulators (Tran & Nguyen, 2024). Taken together, audit experience strengthens auditors’ ability to exercise sound judgment, improves detection of material misstatements, and supports objectivity in audit reporting. Based on this reasoning, the following hypothesis is proposed: H3: Audit experience has a positive relationship with audit quality. 1.4. Team collaboration & audit quality Team collaboration is considered a critical factor influencing audit effectiveness and audit quality. According to Annelin (2024), effective audit teams are characterized by well-coordinated interactions among members, which enables them to process large and complex volumes of information under high-pressure conditions (Salas et al., 2005). The benefits of diverse perspectives can only be realized in a collaborative environment where team members are willing to share knowledge and support one another (Jehn et al., 1999). He et al. (2021) also highlighted that, alongside diversity in experience and expertise, teamwork plays a central role in reconciling individual differences, thereby enhancing objectivity in judgment and reducing the risk of bias. Cameran et al. (2018) emphasized that in the context of audits of listed firms, the degree of collaboration and coordination within audit teams can be a decisive factor in ensuring consistent audit quality. Similarly, research on governance mechanisms also highlights that effective collaboration and monitoring within teams are crucial for sustaining audit quality and meeting stakeholders’ expectations (Baber et al., 2014). He et al. (2021) further provided evidence that collaborative practices among auditors enhance both efficiency and professional skepticism in complex engagements. Nevertheless, ineffective collaboration may also create risks, as conflicts or communication breakdowns can reduce efficiency and hinder consensus- building (Williams & O’Reilly, 1998; Jalagonia et al., 2024). In summary, team collaboration not only facilitates the integration of diverse knowledge and skills but also promotes effective communication and decision-making under complex audit conditions (Tran & Nguyen, 2024; Phan, 2016). Based on this reasoning, the following hypothesis is proposed: H4: Team collaboration has a positive relationship with audit quality. International studies have provided substantial evidence on the relationship between audit team diversity, professional experience, and audit quality (He et al., 2021; Cameran et al., 2018; Annelin, 2024; Williams & O’Reilly, 1998). These works indicate that diversity in cognition, expertise, and experience can enhance error detection, improve objectivity, and strengthen the quality of audit reports. However, most of this evidence has been concentrated in developed markets, where the auditing profession has already reached a high level of professionalization. In contrast, research on audit quality in Vietnam has primarily focused on the individual level, emphasizing auditors’ competence, professional ethics, or emotional intelligence (Doan et al., 2025; Tran & Nguyen, 2024; Phan, 2016). Few studies have approached the issue from the team level, even though audits are typically conducted by teams, and collaboration among members plays a critical role. This gap highlights the need for more empirical evidence on the impact of team-level factors on audit quality in the Vietnamese context—a developing market that is facing increasing pressures of international integration and transparency requirements from regulators Therefore, this study seeks to fill this gap by examining how cognitive diversity, educational and functional diversity, audit experience, and team collaboration affect audit quality in audit teams in Vietnam. Specifically, the study empirically tests four hypotheses regarding the relationship between these team-level factors and audit quality. To test these hypotheses, the study adopts a survey-based research design, which is described in the next section. https://www.malque.pub/ojs/index.php/mr Thuy and Hoai (2026) 4 2. Materials and Methods 2.1. Research model On the basis of the theoretical foundations discussed in the previous section and a synthesis of empirical studies both in Vietnam and internationally, this study proposes a research model to examine the impact of team-level factors on audit quality (AQ) in Vietnamese audit firms. The model tests the relationships between one dependent variable—Audit Quality (AQ)—and four independent variables: (1) Cognitive Diversity (CD), (2) Educational/Functional Diversity (EFD), (3) Audit Experience (AE), and (4) Team Collaboration (TC). The selection of these four factors is grounded in established theories, including cognitive diversity theory, human capital theory, and the team effectiveness model (Page, 2007; Williams & O’Reilly, 1998), and is supported by empirical studies such as Cameran et al. (2018), He et al. (2021), and Annelin (2024). In addition, prior research in emerging markets highlights the challenges of transparency and professionalization in contexts such as Vietnam (Fan & Wong, 2005; Nguyen & Richard, 2011; Doan et al., 2025), which further justify the inclusion of these factors. The hypotheses formulated in the Introduction are tested through this research model, as illustrated in Figure 1 below. Figure 1 Proposed research model. The proposed research model consists of one dependent variable and four independent variables. The dependent variable is Audit Quality (AQ), measured by three observed indicators: (1) the audit team completes the audit on time and in accordance with professional standards; (2) the audit results are considered reliable and useful by clients and relevant stakeholders; and (3) the audit team identifies and addresses material misstatements or potential fraud in the client’s financial statements. These indicators are consistent with prior studies on audit quality (DeAngelo, 1981; Francis, 2011; Cameran et al., 2018; He et al., 2021) and adapted to the Vietnamese context (Doan et al., 2025; Phan, 2016; Tran & Nguyen, 2024). Independent variables: (i) Cognitive Diversity (CD) is measured by five observed indicators: (1) our audit team has different ways of perceiving and approaching the same issue; (2) team members have diverse working styles and problem-solving approaches; (3) I often learn new perspectives from other members of the audit team; (4) cognitive differences among members help the team make more comprehensive audit decisions; and (5) our team encourages diverse viewpoints and professional debate during risk assessment. This scale is adapted from Mello and Rentsch (2015), Cameran et al. (2018), He et al. (2021), and Annelin (2024), reflecting the role of cognitive diversity in enhancing collective judgment and audit quality. (ii) Educational and Functional Diversity (EFD) is measured by four observed indicators: (1) our audit team includes members with different educational backgrounds (e.g., accounting, auditing, finance, information technology, law), (2) team members have prior work experience in various fields before entering the auditing profession, (3) professional diversity in the team enhances our ability to assess clients operating in specialized industries, and (4) multidisciplinary audit teams provide more comprehensive and practical audit solutions. This scale is adapted from Williams and O’Reilly (1998), Simons et al. (1999), and Bonrath & Eulerich (2024). (iii) Audit Experience (AE) is measured by four observed indicators: (1) members of the audit team have different years of auditing experience; (2) the team includes auditors who have worked with various types of clients; (3) members’ experience helps the team identify audit risks more accurately; and (4) the combination of experienced and less experienced members enables the team to achieve more comprehensive audit outcomes. This scale is adapted from Bonner & Lewis (1990), Libby & Frederick (1990), Chi et al. (2016), Cameran et al. (2018), and He et al. (2021), who consistently demonstrate that experienced auditors are better at detecting misstatements and exercising sound judgment. In Vietnam, studies such as Doan et al. (2025) https://www.malque.pub/ojs/index.php/mr Thuy and Hoai (2026) 5 and Phan (2016) have emphasized competence and professional capability at the individual level, indirectly underscoring the importance of audit experience for sustaining audit quality. (iv) Team Collaboration (TC) is measured by four observed indicators: (1) audit team members support each other throughout the audit process; (2) the team consistently shares information in a timely and clear manner across different audit stages; (3) all members are involved in important team discussions and decision-making; and (4) effective collaboration within the team helps minimize errors and ensures audit quality. This scale is adapted from Kozlowski & Ilgen (2006), Mathieu et al. (2008), and Carmeli et al. (2012). The study employs a 5-point Likert scale ranging from “Strongly Disagree” to “Strongly Agree,” defined as follows: (1) Strongly Disagree, (2) Disagree, (3) Neutral, (4) Agree, (5) Strongly Agree. 2.2. Data collection On the basis of the theoretical framework and the proposed research model, a structured quantitative questionnaire was developed to measure the observed variables corresponding to four independent factors and one dependent variable. The questionnaire employed a 5-point Likert scale ranging from 1 (“Strongly Disagree”) to 5 (“Strongly Agree”), comprising 20 items representing 20 observed variables. The survey targeted auditors working on audit teams at medium- and large-sized audit firms in Vietnam. Both senior and junior auditors were included to ensure diversity in terms of roles and experience within the teams. The survey was administered through multiple channels: (i) paper-based distribution at workplaces via human resources departments or audit team leaders, (ii) an online Google Form link sent via company email networks, and (iii) sharing through professional communities on social media platforms, such as the Vietnam Audit Community and ACCA Vietnam groups. A total of 250 questionnaires were distributed. After excluding incomplete or inconsistent responses, the authors retained 198 valid responses for data analysis, resulting in a response rate of 79.2%. 2.3. Data processing The authors used SPSS version 20 to process the data, beginning with descriptive statistical analysis to obtain an overview of the surveyed variables and the distribution trends within the research sample. To assess the reliability of the measurement scales, Cronbach’s alpha was employed to evaluate the internal consistency of the observed variables within each construct. Any item with a corrected item–total correlation below 0.3 was eliminated to ensure scale reliability. Next, exploratory factor analysis (EFA) was conducted to extract latent factors for subsequent analysis. Only variables with factor loadings greater than 0.5 were retained to ensure a representative contribution to each construct. The technical adequacy of the EFA was verified via the Kaiser‒Meyer‒Olkin (KMO) measure, which was required to fall between 0.5 and 1, and Bartlett’s test of sphericity, which needed to reach statistical significance (Significance < 0.05). The principal component analysis (PCA) method combined with varimax rotation was applied to clarify and optimize the factor structure. To estimate the impact of team-level factors—including cognitive diversity, educational/functional diversity, audit experience, and team collaboration—on audit quality, the authors employed multiple linear regression analysis to evaluate the parameters of the proposed research model. 3. Results 3.1. Descriptive statistics The descriptive statistics, which are based on 198 valid survey responses, indicate that the research sample is relatively diverse in terms of age, gender, job position, and employing organization. Specifically, the respondents are auditors working in both domestic and international audit firms of medium to large scale in Vietnam, primarily located in Hanoi and Ho Chi Minh City. Among them, the proportion of female auditors is slightly greater than that of male auditors, reflecting a recent trend toward increased female participation in the auditing profession. Most respondents are between 25 and 35 years old and have 2 to 7 years of auditing experience, representing various roles, including junior, mid-level, and senior auditors. In addition to demographic information, descriptive analysis reflects auditors’ responses to each group of factors in the research model. The mean scores for the observed variables across all the constructs, measured on a 5-point Likert scale, range from 3.6--4.3, indicating a generally positive level of agreement among respondents regarding the team-level factors hypothesized to influence Audit Quality (AQ). Among these, Team Collaboration (TC) and Audit Experience (AE) recorded the highest average scores, suggesting that elements related to internal coordination, trust, and professional experience are highly valued by auditors during the audit process. Meanwhile, the constructs Cognitive Diversity (CD) and Educational/Functional Diversity (EFD) also received moderately high scores, reflecting a positive perception that may still depend on operational mechanisms and team-specific dynamics within individual audit firms. https://www.malque.pub/ojs/index.php/mr Thuy and Hoai (2026) 6 Overall, these findings indicate that auditors recognize the positive role of team-level factors in enhancing audit quality. This provides a strong foundation for testing the causal relationships between the independent variables (CD, EFD, AE, and TC) and the dependent variable (AQ) in the subsequent quantitative analysis. 3.2. Reliability testing The reliability of the measurement scales for team-level factors affecting Audit Quality (AQ) was assessed via Cronbach’s alpha. This test aimed to evaluate the internal consistency among the observed variables within each construct. As shown in Table 1, most of the constructs had Cronbach’s alpha coefficients greater than 0.6, which meets the acceptable threshold for quantitative research in the social sciences. In addition, the corrected item–total correlation values for all the observed variables exceeded 0.3, indicating strong correlations between individual items and their respective latent constructs. Therefore, no items were eliminated during the Cronbach’s alpha testing phase. The reliability criteria were satisfied for the measurement scales of all four independent variables—cognitive diversity (CD), educational/functional diversity (EFD), audit experience (AE), and team collaboration (TC)—as well as the dependent variable Audit quality (AQ). Discussion The findings confirm that team-level factors significantly influence audit quality (AQ) in Vietnamese audit firms. Among them, team collaboration (TC) emerges as the strongest determinant. This aligns with prior evidence that effective collaboration enhances knowledge sharing, mutual support, and coordinated decision-making, thereby reducing bias and improving professional judgment (Carmeli et al., 2012; Mathieu et al., 2008; Cameran et al., 2018; He et al., 2021). In complex engagements, collaboration ensures audit teams maintain consistent quality even under high pressure. Audit experience (AE) is the second strongest factor. This result supports the classic view that experienced auditors provide more accurate judgments and detect misstatements more effectively (Bonner & Lewis, 1990; Libby & Frederick, 1990). At the team level, combining diverse years of practice enhances objectivity and mitigates bias (He et al., 2021; Cameran et al., 2018). Prior work also highlights that experiential capital is a strong predictor of AQ, especially in demanding listed-client audits (Chi et al., 2016; Annelin, 2024). Cognitive diversity (CD) also shows a significant positive association with AQ. This finding echoes arguments that diverse ways of perceiving and approaching issues strengthen audit judgments and reduce groupthink (Mello & Rentsch, 2015; He et al., 2021; Cameran et al., 2018; Annelin, 2024). Encouraging debate and multiple viewpoints during risk assessment thus enhances the reliability of audit outcomes. Educational and functional diversity (EFD) is positively related to AQ, albeit with a smaller effect size. This result supports the view that heterogeneous educational and professional backgrounds expand collective knowledge and improve audit effectiveness when properly integrated (Williams & O’Reilly, 1998; Simons et al., 1999; van Knippenberg & Schippers, 2004; Bonrath & Eulerich, 2024). In Vietnam, however, research has largely emphasized individual-level competence and ethics rather than team-level composition, pointing to a gap in empirical evidence (Doan et al., 2025; Phan, 2016). Overall, the findings reinforce that audit quality is a collective outcome shaped by professional expertise, judgment, and team dynamics (Francis, 2011; Knechel et al., 2015; Cameran et al., 2018; He et al., 2021). They also highlight the need to extend audit research in Vietnam beyond the individual auditor level toward team-based analyses, consistent with international scholarship. 5. Final Considerations https://www.malque.pub/ojs/index.php/mr Thuy and Hoai (2026) 9 This study provides empirical evidence that team-level factors—cognitive diversity, educational/functional diversity, audit experience, and team collaboration—significantly and positively influence audit quality in Vietnamese audit firms. These findings are consistent with international research emphasizing the role of group composition and dynamics in shaping audit outcomes (He et al., 2021; Cameran et al., 2018; Annelin, 2024). By shifting the focus from individual-level determinants, which have dominated domestic research (Doan et al., 2025; Tran & Nguyen, 2024; Phan, 2016), to team-level dynamics, this study bridges a critical gap and contributes to a more comprehensive understanding of audit quality in Vietnam. From a practical perspective, the findings offer several recommendations for audit firms and regulators. First, fostering cognitive and educational/functional diversity within audit teams can enhance judgment quality and reduce bias (He et al., 2021; Cameran et al., 2018; Bonrath & Eulerich, 2024). Second, mentorship and training programs should leverage the audit experience of senior members to build the capabilities of less experienced auditors, thereby strengthening team-level capacity (Bonner & Lewis, 1990; Libby & Frederick, 1990; Chi et al., 2016). Third, encouraging effective collaboration through open communication, knowledge sharing, and participatory decision-making is essential to ensure consistent audit quality (Carmeli et al., 2012; Kozlowski & Ilgen, 2006; Mathieu et al., 2008; Costa, 2003). Finally, regulators and professional bodies could integrate these team-level factors into quality control systems, aligning with international standards and enhancing the credibility of the Vietnamese auditing profession. Despite these contributions, the study has limitations. The sample was restricted to medium- and large-sized firms, which may not fully represent the dynamics of smaller audit practices. The reliance on self-reported survey data also raises the potential for response bias. Future research could address these limitations by adopting longitudinal or multi-method designs, expanding the sample to include smaller firms, and conducting cross-country comparisons. Additionally, examining moderating factors such as organizational culture, leadership styles, or regulatory environments could provide deeper insights into how team-level variables affect audit quality. Qualitative approaches, such as interviews and case studies, may also complement quantitative analyses by uncovering underlying mechanisms. In conclusion, this study advances the literature by empirically validating the impact of team-level factors on audit quality in an emerging market. It reinforces the importance of diversity, experience, and collaboration in audit teams, offering both theoretical and practical contributions. Ultimately, strengthening these dimensions can enhance the objectivity, reliability, and overall quality of audit outcomes, supporting the development of the Vietnamese audit profession and its alignment with global standards. JSON: Name: audit_team_diversity_aq_vn Title: Quantitative survey and multiple regression analysis of team-level determinants of audit quality in Vietnamese audit firms Short Hypothesis: Higher levels of team-level cognitive diversity, educational/functional diversity, audit experience, and team collaboration cause higher audit quality in Vietnamese audit teams. Related Work: Existing work on audit quality falls into three main strands: archival partner- and firm-level analyses using objective outcomes (e.g., restatements, modified opinions) that identify partner identity, firm size, and specialization as predictors; team- and diversity-focused studies in developed markets that use cross-sectional survey or experimental designs to link cognitive and demographic heterogeneity to decision quality; and team-effectiveness literature that emphasizes collaboration, trust, and knowledge sharing. Limitations across these approaches include a dominant focus on individual or firm-level predictors rather than team-level composition and interaction; reliance on single-mode data (either archival or self-report) that creates measurement gaps; limited evidence from emerging markets where auditing practices and professionalization differ; frequent cross-sectional designs that impede causal claims; and small or convenience samples that reduce statistical power and external validity. Additionally, many prior survey studies use subjective audit-quality proxies and suffer from common-method bias and limited robustness checks against objective outcomes. Abstract: This project tests whether team-level characteristics—cognitive diversity, educational/functional diversity, audit experience, and team collaboration—predict audit quality in Vietnamese audit teams. We will collect a stratified survey of auditors in medium and large firms to measure team attributes and perceived audit quality and link survey responses where possible to archival objective outcomes (modified opinions, restatements, or regulatory sanctions) for the same engagements. Measurement scales will be validated with reliability analysis and confirmatory factor models; effects will be estimated with multiple linear regression and multilevel models that control for individual- and firm-level confounders. The main contribution is a rigorous, mixed-source assessment of team composition and interaction as determinants of audit quality in an emerging market, including comparative analyses of subjective versus objective quality measures and ablation tests of each team factor. Expected outcomes include quantified effect sizes for each team determinant and evidence on the relative predictive power of collaboration versus diversity and experience. Experiments: Datasets: (1) Primary cross-sectional survey of auditors employed at medium and large audit firms in Vietnam; target sample N=350-500, stratified by firm size and city (Hanoi, Ho Chi Minh City). Survey items: validated Likert scales for cognitive diversity (5 items), educational/functional diversity (4 items), audit experience (4 items), team collaboration (4 items), and perceived audit quality (3 items). (2) Archival linkage dataset of public-client engagements from the same firms and period: audit opinions (clean/modified), restatements, regulatory sanctions, and client financial statement adjustments for objective AQ proxies. Baselines: Baseline A: individual-level model with auditor demographics and role; Baseline B: firm-level controls (firm size, Big4 status, client industry); Proposed model: individual + firm + team-level predictors; Alternative models: structural equation model (SEM) and multilevel mixed-effects model (auditors nested in teams nested in firms). Evaluation metrics: coefficient estimates and two-tailed p-values, standardized beta coefficients, R-squared and adjusted R-squared, AIC/BIC for model selection, variance inflation factor (VIF) for multicollinearity, intraclass correlation coefficients (ICC) for multilevel models, RMSE for continuous AQ proxies, and AUROC/precision-recall for binary objective AQ outcomes (modified opinion/restatement). Experimental setup: (1) Validate scales via Cronbach's alpha and confirmatory factor analysis (CFA); (2) Run OLS regression of perceived AQ on team predictors with robust standard errors and controls; (3) Run multilevel mixed-effects regression using objective AQ outcomes as dependent variable with team-level predictors at level-2 and firm-level controls at level-3; (4) Robustness checks: replace perceived AQ with archival AQ, include lagged firm-level audit quality, and run propensity-score weighting to adjust for selection into teams. Ablation/comparison studies: (A) Leave-one-predictor-out models to measure marginal contribution of CD, EFD, AE, and TC; (B) Replace team collaboration with interaction terms (e.g., CD*TC, AE*TC) to test moderation; (C) Compare OLS vs. multilevel vs. SEM estimates. Statistical power: compute minimum detectable effect for α=0.05, power=0.8; target N adjusted to detect small-to-medium standardized betas (≈0.2). Risk Factors and Limitations: Measurement and common-method bias: self-reported team attributes and perceived audit quality can induce common-method variance and social desirability. Linkage limitations: inability to match survey responses to archival engagement-level objective outcomes for all respondents reduces triangulation. Causal inference: cross-sectional design limits causal claims and temporal ordering; reverse causality (high-quality teams attract better members) is possible. Sample bias and external validity: focus on medium/large firms and urban centers in Vietnam limits generalization to small firms or other jurisdictions. Statistical power and multicollinearity: small subgroup samples (specific firm types or industries) may lack power; correlated team measures could inflate standard errors despite low VIF in pilot results. Objective AQ measurement limitations: restatements and modified opinions are sparse and may not reflect audit process quality comprehensively. Operationalization risk: aggregating individual responses to team-level constructs may produce aggregation bias if team membership is ambiguous. Computation and scalability: multilevel linkage and SEM on large linked datasets increase computational complexity and require careful model convergence checks.
